questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] cache coherence across layers for a storefront (bazaar, docs/adr/0006-multi-layer-cache-coherence.md). Requirements: 40,000 product pages, each rendered in 3 locales and 3 currencies, are served through a CDN, ISR pages, a Redis cache and Postgres by 12 API instances; merchants change about 2,000 prices an hour, and a changed price must show within 60 seconds on every page that displays it (the product page, its collections and search results); when a flash-sale product's entry expires 10,000 readers ask for it at once; and next month's release changes the shape of the cached product projection. Write your design before you look: what keys and tags look like, the order in which one write's invalidation reaches each layer, what still bounds staleness when an invalidation is lost or races a reader, how concurrent misses are collapsed across instances, how search results stay fresh, and how the new projection shape is rolled out. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Invalidation races the read-through: a reader that missed and loaded the row just before the price change committed stores its result after the invalidation has already deleted the key, so the old price is cached again. The read-through loads, then writes, with no version check, so invalidating after commit narrows this window but cannot close it; only the entry's TTL (or a version compare on write) ends it.

[w3] Register a key under its tags no later than the value is stored: the tagged cache attaches tags only after the read-through has written the value, so an invalidation that lands between the two finds no key under the tag and the stale value survives. Attach tags first, or in the same step as the write.

[w3] Invalidate from the inside out: clear the data cache before revalidating the page, and the page before the CDN, or an outer layer regenerates from a still-stale inner one and stores the old price for a whole new window. The publisher already invalidates entity tags before it revalidates the product path, but nothing in it purges the CDN, so the CDN copy must be purged too or kept short-lived.

[w2] One edit fans out along the dependency graph: the product's tag, plus a tag for each collection it appears in, and every locale-and-currency variant of the page (3 x 3 = 9 keys per product) must be registered under that same product tag, or one variant keeps the old price.

[w2] Search results are keyed by the normalized query, not by entity, so a price change cannot find them through a tag; that is why search gets the shortest TTL (30 seconds, against 120 for collections and 300 for products) as its only freshness mechanism.

[w2] Single-flight here is per process: the in-flight map lives in each instance's memory, so an expiring hot key costs up to one origin load per instance (12, not 1 and not 10,000). That bound is fine for this fleet; a shared lock is only worth its cost when instance count times load cost hurts the origin.

[w2] Roll out a new projection shape by moving to a new key version prefix (the handle-based product key already lives under v2): new code never reads old-shape entries, which age out on their TTL, so no global flush is needed.

[w1] Build keys only from allow-listed parts (a validated handle, a known locale, a known currency, otherwise the default), never from raw headers, cookies or host values, so an attacker cannot mint new cache entries or poison a shared one.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — Black Friday morning on the same design: the deploy went out with a cold cache and a promotion changed which product is hot after the warm list was captured, the invalidation event bus drops events for 10 minutes, the origin times out on every background refresh for 5 minutes, and someone in the incident channel proposes a global cache flush. What breaks, how do you see it, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Failed background refreshes are silent: in the stale window the refresh's error is caught and thrown away and the reader gets the stale value, so for up to the 5-minute stale window nothing reports a problem; once the window ends every reader waits on the failing load. Count refresh failures, because the read path will not tell you.

[w3] A lost invalidation is healed only if the store really expires entries: the in-memory store ignores the TTL it is given, so behind it a missed event means stale forever. Check that the production store enforces expiry before counting on the TTL backstop during the 10-minute event gap.

[w3] A global flush turns every key in every layer cold at the same moment, which is the stampede you were trying to avoid; flush only the poisoned keys or tags, keep single-flight on, warm the hot head, and call it recovered only when hit ratio and database p95 stay in budget for 15 minutes.

[w2] Deploy-time warming used a traffic ranking from before the promotion, so the newly hot product met its first crowd cold; warm the top 50 in batches of 5 on deploy, and add trend warming that warms a key after 20 misses in 10 seconds with a 60-second cooldown.
[w2] Watch keys, not only the total: an overall hit ratio above 90% can hide one hot key that is missing constantly, so alert on a per-key rise in miss rate.

[w2] Replaying the dropped invalidations once the bus recovers reaches tag-indexed entries, but not stale-while-revalidate entries: that store can only get and set, with no delete, so those pages converge only through their fresh and stale windows.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your cache design against the alternatives the ADRs and sprint debates name: event-only versus TTL-only versus both, fine versus coarse keys, waiting for one load versus serving stale while refreshing, an in-process single-flight versus a distributed Redis lock, warming on deploy versus letting the cache fill, adding layers in measured stages versus all at once, and caching admin reads versus bypassing the cache. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Using both events and TTLs buys precision plus self-healing, and the bill is discipline: every write has to name what it invalidates, and the system has to run and monitor two mechanisms instead of one.
keyPoints.quote: Event-only invalidation risks permanent staleness; TTL-only allows predictable lies.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Fine-grained keys (per product, locale and currency) give precise invalidation and a high hit rate per key, but more keys and wider invalidation fan-out; coarse keys mean fewer entries and blunt invalidation with a lower hit rate. Choose per path, from measurements.

[w3] Waiting for one load (single-flight) always returns fresh data but makes the first crowd pay origin latency; serving stale while one refresh runs answers instantly with a value up to the stated window old. Take stale only where that window is acceptable, and keep single-flight beneath it for true misses.

[w2] An in-process single-flight needs no lock service and cannot be stuck behind a dead lock holder, at the price of one load per instance; a distributed Redis lock collapses the fleet to one load but adds a network hop, lock expiry and holder-death rules. The sprint plan promised the Redis lock, while the code ships the in-process map.

[w2] Warming everything wastes deploy time and cache space, and letting the cache fill on its own exposes the database to a cold burst; warm the traffic-ranked head and let the long tail fill on demand behind single-flight.
[w2] Adding layers one measured stage at a time, each with a baseline and a removal rule, shows which layer earns its keep and which is serving stale data; all four at once hides both.

[w1] Admin reads skip the cache on purpose: merchants rarely reread the same thing and need fresh data, and measurement showed no useful shared hit rate, so a cache there would only add a place to be wrong.
